lines.text: High on a stone beam in an Egyptian temple, about three thousand three hundred years old, there is a carving that looks like a helicopter.
Not roughly. It has a rotor on top, a cockpit, and a long tail. Next to it, people see a submarine, a tank and a jet plane.
For more than twenty five years, it has been one of the internet's favourite proofs that ancient Egypt had flying machines. Or visitors who did.
So tonight we treat it the way a forensic lab treats a suspicious document. A questioned document. Every claim is an exhibit, and every exhibit gets examined.
Intake. Photo authentication. Chain of custody. Two hands. The filler. The reading. Comparison specimens.
Then a lab report, with a scorecard and a verdict. Genuine aircraft, or something stranger and far more human. Let's open the file.
Exhibit A arrived, like so many mysteries, by email. In the mid nineteen nineties, photos of the beam were passed around on mailing lists about U F Os and archaeology.
The picture was striking: a neat little helicopter, perfectly outlined, sitting in a line of hieroglyphs as if somebody had carved it from life.
Beside it, other shapes: a long one that looks like a submarine or an airship, and a boxy one that looks like a tank. Below, something like a plane.
The theories followed fast. Egypt had aircraft. Or Atlantis did. Or visitors from the stars showed the priests their machines, and the priests carved what they saw.
Television documentaries picked it up. Websites copied it. In twenty seventeen one viral article added a submarine and even a hoverboard to the list.
One writer searched the phrase and found hundreds of thousands of pages, most of them in favour of ancient flight. The exhibit is famous. Now, is it genuine?
In February nineteen ninety eight, a Belgian U F O researcher named Thierry Wathelet decided to find out. He emailed about fifty Egyptologists and museum curators, and asked.
Examination one: is the photograph honest? A document lab always checks the copy before it checks the original.
The first reply came within hours, from Peter Der Manuelian at Boston's Museum of Fine Arts. What you are looking at, he wrote, is hieroglyphs that have been digitally altered by someone.
Another expert, Jacques Kinnaer, spotted the giveaway. On the temple, the signs are sunken relief, cut into the stone. In the famous close-up, they look raised, almost like bronze.

And the helicopter in that close-up does not quite match the same sign in untouched photos. Its outline has been cleaned up, its edges sharpened, its gaps filled in. Later, versions shown on television were retouched again, to make the craft even more obvious. Each copy drifted a little further from the stone.
So the most famous picture is a retouched picture. But this is where honest investigators slow down, because the story does not end there.
Plenty of tourists have photographed the beam with ordinary cameras. The strange shapes are really there in the stone. The edit exaggerated them. It did not invent them.

Finding one: the viral image is doctored, and that is a point against the claim. But a doctored copy does not prove the original is boring. A real carving still needs a real explanation. So we leave the photographs, and go to the stone itself.
Examination two: chain of custody. Where exactly is this beam, and who made it? It sits in the Temple of Seti the First, at Abydos, in Upper Egypt.
Seti the First ruled Egypt from about twelve ninety four to twelve seventy nine B C. His temple at Abydos was built to honour Osiris, god of the dead, and the king himself.
Its inner reliefs are some of the finest carving anywhere in Egypt. Fine lines, delicate faces, colour still clinging to the stone.
But Seti died before the temple was finished. The job passed to his son, the most famous builder in Egyptian history: Ramesses the Second.

Ramesses ruled for about sixty six years, and few kings ever built more. At Abydos he finished the outer courts and the hypostyle halls, the forests of columns at the front of the temple, and he made sure his own name was everywhere.
And that is where our exhibit lives: on an architrave, a stone beam resting on top of the columns in the first hypostyle hall. Part of the section Ramesses completed.
Scholars note his work there was hurried. Doorways were blocked, the plan was trimmed, the decoration rushed. Egyptologists even have a nickname for him: Ramesses the Chiseler.
Custody since then is well documented. The temple was cleared in the eighteen sixties, then photographed and copied in detail by an expedition that published four volumes by nineteen thirty three.
As one Egyptologist put it, the temple has been intensely studied, copied and published. No unusual hieroglyphs are known. So what is going on up there?
Examination three: two hands. In a document lab, one of the first questions is whether a page was written once, or written over.
There is a word for a surface written on twice: a palimpsest. Medieval scribes scraped old parchment and reused it, and centuries later the first text can still bleed through.
Egyptian builders did the same thing in stone. When a new king took over a monument, he often replaced the old king's names with his own.
In Seti's temple, that is exactly what happened. Ramesses had his father's royal titles on this beam replaced by his own titles. Same spot. Same stone.
Now look at the helicopter with that in mind. According to Egyptologist Peter Brand, it is made from a bow sign from Seti's text, and two arm signs from the text of Ramesses.

Put the two layers on top of each other, and the strokes of one king's words cross the strokes of the other's. The rotor, the cabin and the tail are pieces of two different sentences, written about twenty years apart, by two different teams of carvers who never meant them to touch.
Another Egyptologist, Eugene Cruz Uribe, pointed to the signs for the number nine and for foreign lands, carved one over the other, with parts lost. The tank and submarine come from the same overlap.
Finding two: two different hands, two different reigns, about thirteen hundred B C. The shapes are real, but each stroke belongs to a word.
Examination four: the filler. If Ramesses carved over his father's words, why can we still see both?
The method was simple. The old sunken signs were packed with plaster. When it set, the surface was smooth again, ready to be carved and painted with the new titles.

Painted over, the trick was invisible. Visitors in Ramesses' day would have looked up and seen one clean, colourful inscription, and nothing else. The father's words were still there, but sealed under a skin of plaster.
Then came three thousand years. Paint faded. Parts of the roof collapsed. Weather and time worked on the stone.
And the plaster began to fall out. Wherever it dropped away, Seti's original signs reappeared underneath Ramesses' newer ones. Both texts showing at once.
This is not a one-off. Across the hypostyle hall, column after column shows the names of Seti and Ramesses overlapping. On one, Ramesses even reversed the direction of the writing.

Aidan Dodson, of the University of Bristol, summed it up: the plaster has fallen out, leaving images that look rather like modern items. A Copenhagen scholar called it a perfectly clear case of an ancient correction.

Add erosion of the stone surface, which is visible elsewhere in the temple too, and edges soften into outlines our brains are eager to complete. Finding three: the filler failed, and time did the rest.

Examination five: the reading. Hieroglyphs are not decoration. They are a full writing system with grammar, spelling and fixed formulas, read by scholars every day. So if we read this beam like any other text, what does it actually say?
Every pharaoh had five official names. One of them is called the Two Ladies name, after the vulture goddess and the cobra goddess who protected the king.
Architraves like this one usually carry those royal names, in a fixed order. And every one of the so called flying machines sits inside the Two Ladies names.
Seti's original read, in translation: Powerful of scimitar, who suppresses the Nine Bows. The Nine Bows were Egypt's traditional enemies, bows as in archery.

Ramesses' replacement read: protector of Egypt, who repels foreign lands. A boast written over a boast. Then each text ends with the king's throne name: Menmaatra for Seti, User maatra Setepenra for Ramesses.
This reading is not a guess from the internet. It is set out by Egyptologist Joshua Roberson in a twenty sixteen article, and by Peter Brand in his twenty twenty three book on Ramesses.
Another scholar, Katherine Griffis Greenberg, even gave page numbers in a standard handbook of royal names. The kind of reference you can check yourself.
So the helicopter has a translation. It reads, roughly, Nine Bows meets foreign lands. Finding four: the exhibit is a sentence, not a picture.
Examination six: comparison specimens. A forger's document often fails when you compare it with everything around it. So, what else should exist?

If Egyptians flew helicopters, we would expect the machinery behind them: metal workshops, engines, fuel, spare parts, landing places, crash sites. Egypt is one of the most excavated countries on Earth. Archaeology has found none of it.
Egyptian texts boast about everything: chariots, ships, gold, victories. Not one boasts about flight. And no other tomb or temple shows a helicopter. Only this one beam, and only at this one overlap.
There is a name for what our eyes are doing: pareidolia. The same instinct that finds faces in clouds and electric sockets. It is a feature of the brain, not a flaw of the viewer.

Then there is context. This temple was built to join the dead king with Osiris, so that he would live forever. Its walls are prayers, offerings and royal names. A royal title is the last place a scribe would slip in a picture of a vehicle, and nobody in three thousand years of visitors wrote that they saw one.
And the alien version? It needs visitors who left one doodle in a dead king's name, and nothing else in three thousand years. That is not evidence. It is an overlap with a story attached.
Lab report. Time to score the Abydos helicopter.

A real carved beam in Seti's temple: evidence. Craft-like shapes in untouched photos: real, and a coincidence. Seti's titles under Ramesses' titles: evidence. Plaster that fell out, plus erosion: evidence.
The famous viral photo: retouched. Any supporting trace of aircraft: none. Ancient flight, or alien visitors: debunked.

The verdict. Not a helicopter. Exhibit A is a genuine document that was edited twice: once by a king in about twelve seventy nine B C, and once by someone with photo software in the nineteen nineties.

Somewhere, about three thousand three hundred years ago, a carver working for Ramesses smoothed his plaster over an old king's words and never imagined they would come back. They did. And by pure chance, they look like the future. That is the real mystery of Abydos: not a lost aircraft, but how hungry our eyes are for one.
Next case: stone walls in Scotland that were melted into glass. Ancient lasers, or something much simpler?
What do you see in the beam? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
